description: We built an end-to-end web app that predicts wildfire spread globally in ~1 minute. Users draw an active fire on a map and pick a time horizon to get a probabilistic burn heatmap and spread vectors. Using a physics-based Cellular Automaton (slope, wind, fuel, dryness), it fuses smoke-penetrating radar (NASA NISAR & Canada RCM), thermal satellites (GOES/VIIRS), and Earth Engine data.
summary:
When a wildfire is already burning, crews need to know where it will go in the next hours to decide whom to evacuate and where to hold it. Our system takes the current fire area and returns a map of where the fire is likely to spread, with the main spread direction and estimated arrival times. At its core is a physics-based probabilistic cellular automaton (Alexandridis) driven by slope, wind, vegetation type and density, and dryness. The slow layers (vegetation density, soil moisture, already-burned areas) come from NASA's new NISAR L-band radar, which sees through smoke and cloud. The fast layers come from satellite fire detections (GOES every 5 minutes, VIIRS) and hourly weather from Google Earth Engine.

The app works end to end: draw the fire on a map and get a prediction in about a minute, anywhere in the world. We test it against real 2026 fires in the US and Canada. For each one we built a ground truth of fire progression over time from several satellites, checked against the official perimeter. NISAR's burned-area detection reached 58% overlap (IoU) with the official map. To fill the 12-day gap between NISAR passes, we added RCM, the Canadian Space Agency's radar constellation, which mapped the burned area of a British Columbia fire just 2 days after ignition. Combining the two radars improved burned-area mapping by 8–10 IoU points over either one alone.
details:
What it does. Psapyro predicts where an active wildfire will spread in the next hours. A user draws the burning area on a map, picks a start time, weather source and forecast length, and gets a probability map of where the fire will reach, the main spread direction, expected new burned area and estimated arrival times.

How it works. A probabilistic cellular automaton (Alexandridis et al. 2008) runs Monte Carlo simulations on a 100 m grid, with slope, hourly wind/temperature/humidity, vegetation type and density, fuel moisture, and already-burned areas as inputs. An XGBoost survival model adds arrival-time ranges. Slow layers come from NASA’s NISAR L-band radar (vegetation cover, soil moisture, burn scars); fast layers from GOES (every 5 min) and VIIRS fire detections; terrain, fuel and weather from Google Earth Engine, MERRA-2 and Meteomatics.

Validation. We built a ground truth of fire progression over time for five 2026 fires (Bug CA/NV, Biscar CA, Colwash WA, Crosswhite OR, Bald Range BC) from VIIRS, GOES, NASA FEDS perimeters and official perimeters, and replay the model against it. NISAR burned-area detection reached 58% IoU with the official perimeter on the Bug Fire. To fill NISAR’s 12-day revisit gap we added the Canadian Space Agency’s RADARSAT Constellation Mission (RCM): it mapped the Bald Range burn 2 days after ignition, and NISAR + RCM together improved burned-area mapping by 8–10 IoU points.

Impact. Faster, data-driven evacuation and containment decisions, using radar that sees through smoke and cloud.

Tools. Python (xarray, NumPy, XGBoost), Google Earth Engine, React + MapLibre, GitHub Pages; Claude (SI) for coding assistance and UI mockups.

Creativity / factors. Honest validation against real fires and a naive baseline; combining L-band and C-band radar, which respond in opposite directions to burning.
